ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the horizontal axis is latitude, from 90°N and 70°N on the left, through 0°, to 70°S and 90°S on the right; the vertical labeling is sunrise time, including 3:00, 6:00, 9:00, 12:00, etc. The curve as a whole rises from the high-latitude side of the Northern Hemisphere toward the high-latitude side of the Southern Hemisphere: near about 70°N, the sunrise time is very early, close to the polar day boundary; near the equator, it is around 6 o'clock in the morning; near about 70°S, it rises to 12:00, showing a state close to no sunrise or the polar night boundary. Then reason: The high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere have very early sunrise, and the high latitudes of the Southern Hemisphere are close to polar night, indicating that the direct point of the sun is located in the Northern Hemisphere and that the solar declination is relatively large, close to the period around the summer solstice. According to the relationship of the polar day and polar night boundary, |latitude| + |solar declination| ≈ 90°, and the boundary is around 70°, so the solar declination can be estimated to be about 20°N, close to 23.5°N at the summer solstice on June 22. Combining that the figure reflects the midsummer situation in the Northern Hemisphere shortly after the summer solstice, this day might be early July.

<image1>

method.method_draft: First describe the image: the sunrise-time curve along 120°E rises from the Northern Hemisphere side to the Southern Hemisphere side, with very early sunrise near 70°N and about 12:00/no sunrise boundary near 70°S. Then infer that the Arctic side is experiencing polar day while the Antarctic side is experiencing polar night. Use the polar-circle relation |φ|+|δ|≈90° to estimate a large positive solar declination, close to the June-solstice value. Convert that seasonal position to a calendar date and choose the plausible time shortly after the solstice: 7月初.
